analogy.p: Imagine a lawn with mostly ordinary grass and a few weeds that happen to be immune to weedkiller. Spraying kills the ordinary grass but not the immune weeds, which then spread into the bare soil and take over the lawn. The weedkiller did not create the immune weeds; it just removed the competition, just as antibiotics select resistant bacteria. It breaks down because bacteria reproduce in minutes and exchange no seeds, and because the lawn does not spread diseases to people.

bullets: **Pathogen** = a microorganism that causes disease; bacteria are one type of pathogen.
**Antibiotic** = a drug that kills bacteria (or stops them growing) inside the body; antibiotics do **not** work on viruses.
**Resistant strain** = a form of the bacterium that is **not killed** by a particular antibiotic.
The whole topic is **natural selection** applied to a very fast-reproducing organism.
Key examples: **MRSA** (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus), a bacterium resistant to many antibiotics.
The exam links this to **evolution** (theory of natural selection) and to **health** (treating infectious disease).
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: The AQA specification (4.6.3 Evolution) says that **bacteria can evolve rapidly because they reproduce at a fast rate**, that **mutations of bacterial pathogens produce new strains**, and that some strains may be **resistant to antibiotics** and so are **not killed**. You must be able to explain how resistance spreads as an example of **natural selection**, name **MRSA**, and describe how the rate of development of resistant strains can be reduced. This is a popular 4 to 6 mark question because it tests whether you can write a logical chain of cause and effect.

bullets: Bacteria **reproduce asexually** by binary fission, so each division makes two genetically identical cells (unless a mutation occurs).
Short **generation time** (as little as 20 minutes) means the **population grows exponentially**: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and so on.
A huge population means that even a **very rare mutation** will happen in some cell somewhere.
More generations in a given time = more chances for **mutation** and more rounds of **selection**.
This is why antibiotic resistance can appear within **years** of a new antibiotic being used widely.
Compare with slow-breeding organisms such as elephants or oak trees, where evolution is much slower in human timescales.
core.p: Evolution is a change in the inherited characteristics of a population over many generations. The speed of evolution depends partly on how many generations occur in a given time. Bacteria can **divide by binary fission as often as once every 20 minutes** when conditions are good, so a population can go through dozens of generations in a single day. A human generation takes about 25 years, so bacteria can show changes in days or weeks that would take us thousands of years.

bullets: Mutations are **random**: bacteria do not 'decide' to become resistant, and the antibiotic does not make them mutate in a useful direction.
A resistance mutation may change the **target protein** the antibiotic attacks, or let the cell **destroy or pump out** the drug (extra detail, not required at GCSE).
Because the population is enormous, there is often **already** a tiny number of resistant cells **before** the antibiotic is ever used.
The mutated allele is **inherited**: when the resistant cell divides, **both daughter cells are resistant**.
**New strain** = a genetically different version of the pathogen with a new characteristic.
Mark scheme phrase: 'a **mutation** occurs, producing a **new strain** which is **resistant** to the antibiotic'.
core.p: A **mutation** is a **random change in the DNA** (base sequence) of an organism. When a bacterium copies its DNA before dividing, mistakes occasionally happen. Most mutations have no effect or are harmful, but a few change the **phenotype** in a useful way. A mutated pathogen that behaves differently from the original is called a **new strain**. Mutations are **random** and are **not caused by the antibiotic**: the antibiotic simply **selects** for a resistance mutation that was already there.

bullets: Step 1: **Variation** exists because a random mutation produces a resistant bacterium among many non-resistant ones.
Step 2: The **antibiotic is used**, which is the **selection pressure**.
Step 3: **Non-resistant bacteria are killed**; the **resistant bacterium survives** (survival of the fittest in this environment).
Step 4: The survivor **reproduces** (binary fission), passing the **resistance allele** to its offspring.
Step 5: Within a few generations the **population is made up mainly of resistant bacteria**.
Step 6: The antibiotic is now **ineffective** and the infection is much harder to treat.
This is the same logic as Darwin's theory: **variation, competition/selection, survival, reproduction, inheritance**.
core.h: Natural selection of resistant bacteria: step by step
core.p: You need to be able to describe resistance spreading as natural selection. In a population of bacteria there is **variation** because of mutation. When an antibiotic is used, it creates a **selection pressure**: bacteria without resistance are **killed**, but the resistant ones **survive**. The survivors face **less competition** and **reproduce**, passing on the **resistance allele**. Over time the **proportion of resistant bacteria increases** until the antibiotic stops working.

bullets: Number of bacteria after n divisions = **starting number × 2^n**.
Number of divisions = **total time ÷ generation (division) time**.
Example: 1 cell, division every 20 min, 2 hours: 120 ÷ 20 = **6 divisions**, so 2^6 = **64 cells**.
Graph of number against time is a **curve that gets steeper**, not a straight line.
Fast growth means the resistant strain can **dominate the population before the infection is noticed**.
Spread between people (e.g. in hospitals) makes resistant strains a **public health** problem, not just a problem for one patient.
core.h: The speed of spread: exponential growth
core.p: Once a single resistant bacterium has survived, it can produce a huge population very fast because of **exponential growth**. If a bacterium divides every 20 minutes, the number doubles each time: after n divisions you have **2 to the power n** cells (starting from one cell). This is why a single survivor in a patient can become billions within a day, and why resistant bacteria then **spread from person to person** (by touch, coughs, hospital surfaces) before doctors can react.

bullets: **MRSA** is the example named in the specification: a bacterium **resistant to antibiotics**.
It arose by **mutation then natural selection** in an environment where antibiotics were used a lot.
Hospitals are 'hotspots' because of heavy antibiotic use, vulnerable patients and close contact.
Control of spread: **hand washing**, **alcohol gels**, **isolating infected patients**, **sterilising equipment**, **screening patients**.
Infections can often only be treated with a **few remaining 'last resort' antibiotics**.
Do not say MRSA is a virus: it is a **bacterium**, so it has nothing to do with viral infections.
core.p: **MRSA** stands for **methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus**. Staphylococcus aureus is a common bacterium that lives harmlessly on many people's skin but can cause serious infections of wounds, blood and lungs. Mutation produced strains resistant to methicillin and then to many other antibiotics, so MRSA is a **resistant strain** that is difficult to treat. It is particularly dangerous in **hospitals**, where patients have open wounds and weakened immune systems, and where antibiotics are used heavily, giving a strong selection pressure.

bullets: **Not immune**: the strain is new, so almost nobody has antibodies or memory cells for it.
**No effective treatment**: the antibiotic that would normally kill it has no effect, so patients stay infectious for longer.
Spread is quickest where people are close together or already weak, such as **hospitals** and care homes.
Each infected person acts as a source of more resistant bacteria, so the **proportion of resistant bacteria in the population rises**.
The same logic applies to other resistant pathogens, not only **MRSA**.
Control spread with **hygiene** (hand washing, alcohol gel), **isolation of patients** and **screening**.
Do not mix up words: bacteria are **resistant** to antibiotics, people are **immune** to a pathogen.
core.h: Why a resistant strain spreads and why it is hard to stop
core.p: The specification says that once a resistant strain exists, **the resistant strain will spread because people are not immune to it and there is no effective treatment**. Being immune means your immune system already has memory cells against that pathogen, which is usually gained by catching the disease or by vaccination. A newly arisen strain looks different to the immune system, so most people have no protection, and the usual antibiotic that would help the body fight it no longer works. The strain therefore passes from person to person, through coughs, touch and contaminated surfaces, much faster than doctors can respond, and it can become common in a population.

bullets: Antibiotics kill **bacteria**, not viruses (viruses can be prevented with **vaccines**, and some treated with antiviral drugs).
Antibiotics specifically target a particular **type** of bacteria, so the right one must be chosen.
Taking antibiotics for a viral infection gives **no benefit** to the patient.
It still exposes the patient's harmless bacteria to **selection pressure**, which can create resistant strains.
Doctors may take a sample and test which antibiotic works (a **sensitivity test**) before prescribing a narrow-spectrum drug.
Link to other topics: **communicable diseases**, **vaccination**, **monoclonal antibodies**.
core.h: Why antibiotics do not work on viruses
core.p: Antibiotics work by attacking features that bacteria have, such as their **cell walls** or the way they make proteins. **Viruses are not living cells**; they live and reproduce **inside host cells**, so antibiotics cannot target them without also harming the patient's own cells. That is why antibiotics must **not** be prescribed for colds, flu or most sore throats, which are usually viral. Using antibiotics when they cannot help only gives bacteria in the body more chances to be selected for resistance.

bullets: **Doctors should not prescribe antibiotics inappropriately**, for example for **non-serious infections** or **viral infections** such as colds.
**Patients should complete the full course** of antibiotics so that **all bacteria are killed** and none survive to mutate and form resistant strains.
**Agricultural use of antibiotics should be restricted**, because routinely feeding antibiotics to farm animals exposes huge numbers of bacteria to selection pressure.
Good **hygiene** and **isolation** reduce spread, so fewer infections need treating.
**Rotating or combining** antibiotics and using a narrow-spectrum drug where possible lowers the chance of survival (extra detail).
Reasoning to include: 'fewer bacteria exposed to the antibiotic, so **less chance of a resistant mutant surviving and reproducing**'.
core.h: How to reduce the rate of development of resistant strains
core.p: The specification lists three measures. We cannot stop resistance appearing altogether because mutation is random and natural selection is unavoidable, but we can **slow it down** by reducing the **selection pressure** and the number of times bacteria are exposed to antibiotics. All three measures work by the same logic: fewer exposures and complete killing give resistant bacteria fewer chances to survive and reproduce.

bullets: Feeling better does **not** mean every bacterium is dead.
Survivors are those **most able to tolerate** the antibiotic, so they are already a selected group.
Stopping early lets them **multiply** and pass on their tolerance, so the next infection needs a stronger drug.
Resistant bacteria can also be **passed to other people**.
Model phrase: 'to kill **all** the bacteria so that **none survive to mutate** and produce a resistant strain'.
Do not just say 'so they get better': the mark is for the **link to resistance**.
core.h: Why patients must finish the course
core.p: A common 4 mark question asks why patients should complete a course even when they feel better. After a few days the antibiotic has killed most bacteria, so the symptoms fade. But the **most resistant or least susceptible bacteria may still be alive**. If the patient stops early these survivors **reproduce**, and the infection returns in a form that is **harder to kill**. Completing the course ensures **all bacteria are killed**, including any partially resistant ones.

bullets: New drug development is **costly**: research, trials, safety testing, approval.
It is **slow**: often 10 or more years from discovery to patients.
Bacteria reproduce so fast that resistance to any new drug may appear **soon after it is introduced**.
Therefore **prevention** (using existing antibiotics carefully) is as important as discovering new ones.
Link to **drug testing** (preclinical and clinical trials) in the health topic.
Risk: a future with **no effective antibiotics**, where routine operations and minor infections become dangerous again.
core.p: The specification states that **the development of new antibiotics is costly and slow**, and that it is **unlikely to keep up with the emergence of new resistant strains**. A new drug takes many years of research, testing and clinical trials, costing hundreds of millions of pounds, and pharmaceutical companies earn less from antibiotics (taken for short courses) than from drugs taken for life. Meanwhile bacteria evolve resistance in months or years, so we are in a constant race that bacteria can win.

bullets: It is evolution you can **see** within a human lifetime or even a lab session.
It shows that **selection pressure** (the antibiotic) changes the **allele frequency** in the population.
It shows variation arises by **random mutation**, not by need or intention.
Compare with **peppered moths** and other textbook examples that take longer or are harder to observe.
Hospitals show it on a large scale: the more an antibiotic is used, the more resistance is found.
Link to **Theories of evolution** and **Genetics**: alleles, mutation, inheritance.
core.p: Antibiotic resistance is one of the best **observable examples of evolution by natural selection** happening in real time. Because bacteria reproduce so fast, scientists can watch a population change within days in the lab: a plate of bacteria treated with an antibiotic is left with only the resistant colonies. It supports Darwin's ideas: **variation exists, the environment selects, survivors reproduce and pass on advantageous alleles**.

bullets: Quote **values from the graph** (e.g. 'rose from 5% to 40% in 6 years') and calculate **change** or **percentage change** where asked.
Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100.
Describe the **shape**: a curve getting steeper suggests exponential growth.
If resistant numbers rise after antibiotic use rises, say it is **consistent with** natural selection.
If the graph shows total population falling but resistant numbers rising, explain that **non-resistant bacteria died** and the **resistant ones survived**.
Check axis **labels and units** (minutes, hours, millions per cm³) before quoting.
core.h: Interpreting data and graphs about resistance
core.p: Questions often give a table or graph showing antibiotic use against percentage of resistant bacteria, or bacterial numbers over time. Describe what happens using **numbers with units**, identify the **trend**, and explain it using natural selection. Be careful to distinguish **correlation** (both rise together) from **causation** (use of antibiotics causes the selection); a good answer says the data **suggest** a link, supported by the known mechanism.

bullets: Sterilise **Petri dishes and agar** (e.g. in an autoclave) and flame the **inoculating loop** to kill unwanted microbes.
**Tape the lid** loosely (do not seal fully) so no harmful anaerobic bacteria grow.
Incubate at about **25 °C** in school labs (not 37 °C, which could encourage human pathogens to grow).
Measure the **diameter of each clear zone** and calculate **area = π × r²**.
Control variables: **same bacteria, same agar depth, same disc size, same concentration, same incubation time and temperature**.
Safety: wash hands, disinfect surfaces, dispose of dishes by autoclaving.
core.h: Required-style reasoning: testing antibiotics in the lab
core.p: Although the culturing bacteria practical belongs to microbiology, the **same idea** appears here. Bacteria are grown on agar jelly in a Petri dish, and discs soaked in different antibiotics are placed on it. A **clear zone (inhibition zone)** around a disc shows bacteria were killed; a **bigger clear zone** means a more effective antibiotic. Resistant bacteria grow right up to the disc. Good technique matters: **aseptic technique** prevents contamination by unwanted microbes that could be dangerous.

exam: **Command words:** 'Describe' = say what happens; 'Explain' = say what happens AND why using science; 'Suggest' = apply knowledge to an unfamiliar situation.
**1-2 mark recall:** 'Why should doctors not prescribe antibiotics for viral infections?' → 'Antibiotics do not kill viruses' **and** 'overuse can lead to resistant bacteria'.

**Typical 4 mark 'explain how resistant strains develop':** mutation produces a resistant bacterium → antibiotic kills non-resistant bacteria → resistant bacteria survive and reproduce → resistant allele passed on, population becomes mainly resistant.
**6 mark answers:** structure as a chain (mutation, selection pressure, survival, reproduction, inheritance, spread) and then add a **measure to reduce resistance** with reasoning.
**Use the key words** 'mutation', 'resistant', 'survive', 'reproduce', 'pass on', 'allele'. Examiners reward the exact chain.
**Calculations:** doubling questions need number of divisions = time ÷ division time, then 2^n. Show the working line.
**Graphs:** quote two data points with units, describe the trend, then link to selection. Do not simply say 'it goes up'.
**Evaluate/justify questions:** give a benefit and a limitation, e.g. restricting farm antibiotics reduces selection pressure but may raise food costs or animal disease.
**Check the 'Suggest why' questions:** hospitals have heavy antibiotic use, vulnerable patients and close contact, so resistant strains spread fast.

mistakes.r: Resistance arises by **random mutation** that exists independently of the antibiotic; the antibiotic **selects** the resistant bacteria.
mistakes.w: Bacteria become resistant because the antibiotic makes them mutate, or they get used to it.

mistakes.r: The **bacteria** are resistant, not the person. Individual bacteria do not adapt: the **population** changes by natural selection.
mistakes.w: The bacteria adapt to the antibiotic / the person becomes resistant.

mistakes.r: Name it properly: **non-resistant bacteria are killed**, **resistant bacteria survive and reproduce**, passing on the **resistance allele**.
mistakes.w: The antibiotic kills the weak bacteria and the strong ones survive.

mistakes.r: Antibiotics only work on **bacteria**, not viruses; using them for viruses is inappropriate.
mistakes.w: Antibiotics should be used for viral infections like colds.

mistakes.r: Finish the course so that **all bacteria are killed** and none survive to **mutate and form resistant strains**.
mistakes.w: Finish the course so you get better.

mistakes.r: MRSA is a **strain of bacterium** (Staphylococcus aureus) resistant to methicillin and other antibiotics.
mistakes.w: MRSA is a virus / a superbug that is a disease itself.

mistakes.r: New antibiotics are **costly and slow** to develop and are **unlikely to keep up** with new resistant strains.
mistakes.w: We can just make new antibiotics when resistance appears.

mistakes.r: They evolve fast because they **reproduce rapidly** (short generation time), giving many generations and more chances for mutation and selection.
mistakes.w: Bacteria evolve fast because they are simple.

mistakes.r: Bacteria are **resistant** to antibiotics; **immune** is used for people who are protected against a pathogen.
mistakes.w: The resistant bacteria are immune to the antibiotic.

summary: The specification asks you to explain that bacteria evolve quickly because they reproduce fast, that mutation produces new strains, and that resistant strains such as MRSA survive antibiotics and spread by natural selection. You must also describe how to reduce resistance and why new antibiotics cannot easily keep up; it matters because it is both a classic evolution example and a major health issue.

terms.d: A drug that kills bacteria or prevents their growth; it does not work against viruses.
When bacteria are not killed by an antibiotic because of a genetic change.
A form of a bacterial pathogen that is not killed by a particular antibiotic.
A random change in the DNA of an organism that may produce a new characteristic.
A genetically distinct variety of a pathogen.
The process by which organisms best suited to their environment survive and reproduce, passing on their alleles.
An environmental factor, such as an antibiotic, that makes some individuals more likely to survive than others.
Asexual reproduction in which a bacterial cell divides into two identical cells.
Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus: a bacterium resistant to many antibiotics.
Differences between individuals of the same species, caused by genes and environment.
A change in the inherited characteristics of a population over time, through natural selection, which may result in a new species.
The full set of doses prescribed by a doctor to kill all the bacteria.
Growth in which the number doubles in equal time periods, so it rises faster and faster.
A clear area on an agar plate around an antibiotic disc where bacteria have not grown.
A mutant version of a gene that makes a bacterium resistant to an antibiotic; it is passed to daughter cells.
Protected against a pathogen because the immune system already has memory cells for it (people are immune, bacteria are resistant).
Methods such as sterilising equipment and flaming the loop that stop unwanted microbes contaminating a culture.

worked.ans: A mutation in a bacterium makes it resistant. The antibiotic kills the non-resistant bacteria, but the resistant bacterium survives and reproduces. It passes on the allele for resistance to its offspring, so over time most of the population is resistant and the antibiotic no longer works (natural selection).
worked.q: Explain how a strain of bacteria can become resistant to an antibiotic. (4 marks)
steps: Mark 1: A random mutation produces a bacterium that is resistant to the antibiotic.
Mark 2: When the antibiotic is used, non-resistant bacteria are killed.
Mark 3: The resistant bacterium survives and reproduces.
Mark 4: The resistance allele is passed on, so the population becomes mainly resistant.

worked.ans: Not all the bacteria have been killed. The survivors can reproduce and pass on resistance, so a resistant strain could develop and be passed to other people, making a future infection harder to treat.
worked.q: A patient is given a 7 day course of antibiotics but stops after 3 days because they feel better. Explain why this is a problem. (3 marks)
steps: Some bacteria may still be alive.
These may be the ones least affected by the antibiotic.
They can reproduce and pass on their tolerance or resistance.
